newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan officials hold second day of talks.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan officials hold second day of talks.

text.p: Indian and Pakistani officials held talks shrouded in secrecy for a second day on Saturday with no sign yet that the arch-rivals had narrowed differences over the volatile Himalayan territory of Kashmir.

Earlier on Saturday Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda briefly met negotiators from both sides at his residence. Shamshad Ahmad, Pakistan's foreign secretary, and his Indian opposite number Salman Haidar later resumed talks they began on Friday.
The two sides have agreed to make no public comment until their discussions, due to end on Monday, are over.
But the Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency said Ahmad had told Deve Gowda Pakistan would not put the thorny Kashmir dispute on hold while the two countries discuss other problems.

"There has to be some meaningful progress on the core issue of Kashmir before we address other matters," PTI quoted Ahmad as telling Deve Gowda. There was no official confirmation of Ahmad's reported remarks.
PTI said the Indian delegation had stressed New Delhi's refusal to consider anything that would disturb India's secular unity and jeopardise its sovereignty (over Kashmir).
It quoted a senior Pakistani official said as saying that if India even agreed that Kashmir was a dispute, "that itself will show that some progress has been achieved".
PTI said the two sides were getting bogged down on setting an agenda, with Pakistan insisting on progress on Kashmir and India proposing a "step-by-step approach" to the issue.

India had suggested confidence-building measures in trade, culture and people-to-people contacts, PTI said. It also proposed extending an existing agreement not to attack each other's nuclear installations to cities and economic targets.

The talks are the first since January 1994, when a dialogue foundered on Kashmir. Tension over the disputed Himalayan region sparked two of the three wars the two countries, now threshold nuclear powers, have fought since independence in 1947.
India accuses Pakistan of sponsoring Moslem Kashmiri guerrillas fighting Indian rule for the past seven years in the two thirds of Kashmir controlled by New Delhi.
Pakistan, which holds the rest of Kashmir, denies the charge, but says it supports the Kashmiris politicallly.

Kashmiri separatists in the umbrella Hurriyat organisation staged a strike in Srinagar for a second day on Saturday to protest at their exclusion from the talks. Witnesses said shops closed in the city, the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir.
Shabir Ahmad Shah, a separatist leader detained on Friday during a march by 100 Hurriyat supporters, was later released.
Police also detained, and later freed, a dozen Hurriyat leaders, including the group's chairman Mirwaiz Omar Farooq, in New Delhi to block a planned protest near the talks venue.
Farooq said the All Parties Hurriyat (freedom) Conference did not oppose rapprochement between India and Pakistan, but wanted Kashmiris to be part of any talks on their homeland.
"We don't see this as a bilateral issue," he told Reuters by telephone. "It's not a territorial or regional dispute they can discuss by themselves...The Kashmiris must be involved."
The governor of Jammu and Kashmir, K.V. Krishna Rao, said Pakistan should show its sincerity by reining in the guerrillas.

"Pakistan should stop infiltrating militants into Kashmir and hand over the Kashmiri youths undergoing training in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir to India to give peace a chance to flourish," PTI quoted him as telling 200 former militants who have joined the paramilitary border security force.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in Kashmir since the start of an armed revolt there in January 1990.
